q: At what point in the cycle does a classified chateau normally settle the proportions of its grand vin?
opts: Only after the first year's sales figures are known
Immediately before bottling, about two years after the harvest
In the winter or spring after the harvest
At the press, so the varieties ferment together
exp: Lots are fermented and kept separate by variety and by parcel, then tasted and assembled early, so what the trade tastes in the spring is already the blend. The lots left out go to the second wine or are sold off in bulk.

q: Drawing clear wine off its sediment from one barrel to another, a cellarman sets a lit candle behind the glass to watch for the first cloud. Name the operation.
exp: Racking every three months or so in the first year both clarifies the wine and gives it a measured dose of air, which softens tannin. The candle is the oldest gauge there is: the moment the stream turns hazy, the cellarman stops.

q: Classified-growth reds are still clarified before bottling with a traditional agent whipped up at five or six per barrique. What is that agent?
exp: The albumen binds the harshest tannins and carries them to the bottom, softening the wine without stripping it the way a heavy filtration would. It is one reason a classified Bordeaux is not usually vegan, and estates that skip it now often bottle unfined instead.

q: Bordeaux has a traditional-method sparkling appellation of its own, and the rules set a floor for time on the lees. How long?
exp: Cremant de Bordeaux is made from the region's own varieties, whites and reds alike, and the nine-month floor is the standard Cremant requirement across France. Non-vintage Champagne must spend twelve months on its lees inside a fifteen-month minimum before release, which is a fair measure of how much of that category's character is bought with time.

q: Grapes left to raisin on the vine also concentrate their sugar. What does noble rot do beyond that?
opts: It raises the total acidity of the juice
It removes the need for a selective harvest
It adds tannin drawn out of the skins
It consumes tartaric acid and leaves glycerol
exp: Passerillage is pure dehydration, so the juice is simply a more concentrated version of what was there. Botrytis is an organism living in the berry: it eats into the tartaric acid, and it leaves behind glycerol, gluconic acid and the honeyed, saffron aromas of its own that raisined fruit never shows.

q: Sauternes and Barsac name two of the five communes entitled to the appellation. Name the three others.
exp: Yquem is in Sauternes, Rieussec and de Fargues in Fargues, and La Tour Blanche and Lafaurie-Peyraguey in Bommes. Only Barsac holds the right to a name of its own, and the other four have to use the collective one.

q: Let the autumn stay wet and the same fungus becomes a disaster instead of an asset. What is the destructive form called?
exp: Without dry afternoons the berry never dehydrates, so the fungus keeps spreading, splits the skins and lets acetic bacteria and fruit flies in. The finished wine tastes mouldy and oxidised, which is why a single week of the wrong weather can cost a Sauternes estate its whole crop.

q: Between Barsac and the city of Bordeaux, enclaved inside Graves on the same side of the river, lies a third sweet-wine appellation whose growers may also sell dry wine as Graves. Name it.
exp: It sits within the Graves boundary rather than beside it, so a grower there has two appellations available depending on how the wine finishes. The style is lighter and less sweet than Sauternes, which makes it a useful half-step between a dry Graves and a full Sauternes on a list.

q: Botrytised must settles poorly and blocks a filter almost at once, because the fungus leaves a sticky polysaccharide behind in the juice. Name that compound.
exp: The molecule is long and gelatinous, so it bridges the pores of a pad or membrane the moment pressure is applied. Cellars deal with it by settling the must cold and long, or with a glucanase enzyme, rather than by pushing harder.

q: Serious dry white Bordeaux is usually denied one conversion that every red in the region undergoes. Which, and for what reason?
opts: Malolactic conversion, blocked to preserve acidity
Alcoholic fermentation, stopped early to leave a little sugar
Cold stabilisation, skipped so tartrates remain
Oxidative racking, avoided so no air reaches the wine
exp: Malic acid is the sharper of the two, and in a maritime climate where whites are picked for freshness it is worth keeping. Chilling the barrel and a dose of sulphur are the usual means, and where the wine is left to go through it, richness is being chosen over tension.

q: Through the first winter a white barrel is opened and its sediment stirred back up into the wine. What is that operation called?
exp: Suspended lees give body and a creamy texture and also consume oxygen, so a stirred barrel is better protected than a still one. Overdone it flattens the aromatics, which is why estates chasing precision now stir far less than they did a generation ago.

q: Graves Superieures on a label promises something other than a better dry white. What is actually in the bottle?
exp: The word Superieures marks style, not rank: the appellation is reserved for white with residual sugar from the Graves zone. A guest who orders it expecting a grander version of dry Graves gets a semi-sweet wine, which is a good reason to read the word out loud when the bottle is presented.

q: Grapefruit and boxwood in a young Sauvignon Blanc come from sulphur-bearing compounds that are locked in the grape and released by the yeast. Name that family of compounds.
exp: They exist in the fruit bound to other molecules and have no smell until fermentation cuts them loose, which is why the choice of yeast changes the aroma so much. They also oxidise readily, and their loss is much of what makes an old bottle of cheap Sauvignon taste of nothing in particular.

q: A customer buys a case as futures in the spring after the harvest. What has he paid for, and when does it arrive?
opts: Wine still in barrel, paid for now and delivered in bottle about two years later
A share of the vintage settled in cash rather than in wine
Bottled wine already in the chateau's own cellar, held there until he calls for it
An option to buy later at whatever the market price turns out to be
exp: The money reaches the chateau long before the wine is bottled, which is the whole commercial point of the system. The buyer takes the risk that the wine will be cheaper on release, and the price is normally quoted in bond, so duty and VAT still fall due when the wine is taken out of the warehouse.

q: Standing between a chateau and the merchant who buys from it is a second intermediary who never takes ownership of the wine. What does that party do?
opts: Sets the release price and announces it to the market
Brokers the sale and samples the wine for a small commission
Bottles and labels the wine on the chateau's behalf
Buys the wine outright and resells it at a margin
exp: The courtier knows both cellars and books, matches wine to merchant and guarantees the sample matches the lot, and takes about two percent for it. The negociant is the one taking title and risk, and the chateau alone sets the price.

q: Merchants on the Place cannot simply order what they want from a sought-after chateau; a house holds a fixed share of the crop, year in and year out. What is that entitlement called?
exp: The share is historic and jealously guarded, and a merchant who declines a poor vintage risks losing it in a good one. That is why weak years still sell: the entitlement, not the wine, is what the buyer is protecting.
